Satan's rage is the rage of the defeated; his time (kairos) is limited. Whether the 'short time' is the 3.5-year period that follows or the whole interval between ascension and return depends on one's wider framework.
The brief period up to AD 70 (and Nero's death) in which Satan vents his fury on the church and Israel.
The final three and a half years before Christ's return.
The whole church age, short from God's perspective.
The woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly to her place in the wilderness

God says he bore Israel out of Egypt 'on eagles' wings' (Exodus 19:4) and is like an eagle that carries its young (Deuteronomy 32:11); those who wait on the LORD mount up with wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:31). The image is a new exodus.
The eagle was Jupiter's bird and the standard (aquila) of the Roman legions; some commentators suggest an ironic contrast, though John's explicit allusion is to Exodus.
God himself rescues and carries his people, as he did at the exodus. The passive 'was given' points to divine action. The verse repeats and expands 12:6.
The serpent spewed water like a river; the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river

Floods are a stock image for overwhelming enemies (Psalm 18:4, 16; 32:6; 124:2-5; Isaiah 43:2). The earth opening its mouth recalls Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16:30-32) and the Song of the Sea, where 'the earth swallowed them' (Exodus 15:12). Pharaoh, the Nile dragon, tried to destroy Israel's sons in the river (Exodus 1:22).

Asia Minor was a land of rivers that vanished into limestone sinkholes, and earthquakes regularly opened the ground; such phenomena would make the picture vivid, though it is not a specific local reference.

Satan tries to sweep God's people away with a torrent (persecution, slander or deceptive teaching, since the water comes from his mouth), but creation itself is enlisted to protect them. The scene again reworks the exodus.
Persecution and armies sent against the Jewish-Christian church in Judea, frustrated by providence (Chilton).
Often the barbarian invasions or waves of persecution against the faithful church, absorbed or turned aside (Elliott, Barnes).
Possibly a literal flood or army sent against the fleeing Jewish remnant, thwarted by a supernatural intervention (Walvoord).
The flood of lies, false teaching and persecution that comes from Satan's mouth in every age, from which God preserves the church (Beale, Hendriksen).
The rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus

Genesis 3:15 promises enmity between the serpent and the woman's 'seed'; the woman's seed is here both Messiah and his brothers and sisters (Hebrews 2:11-13). Keeping the commandments is covenant language (Exodus 20:6; Deuteronomy 7:9).

Having failed to destroy the Messiah and the protected woman, the dragon targets the individual believers who are her children. Interpreters debate whether the woman and her 'rest of offspring' are distinguished (e.g. Jewish and Gentile believers, or the ideal church and actual believers) or the same people seen from two angles.
The Gentile churches beyond Judea, persecuted under Nero after the Jewish-Christian 'woman' was protected (Gentry, Chilton).
Believers of the tribulation period, including Gentiles and Jews not among the protected remnant (Walvoord, Thomas).
Individual Christians on earth, as distinct from the church as a heavenly, protected entity (Beale).
The dragon stood on the shore of the sea

The sea is the home of chaos and of Daniel's beasts (Daniel 7:2-3); in Job 40-41 Leviathan dwells in the sea and Behemoth on land, a pairing echoed in 1 Enoch 60:7-9, 4 Ezra 6:49-52 and 2 Baruch 29:4.

From the province of Asia, Roman power arrived over the sea: proconsuls landed each year at Ephesus. Some manuscripts (followed by the KJV, as 13:1) read 'I stood', placing John on the shore instead; the best manuscripts read 'he stood'.

The dragon takes his stand at the sea's edge to summon a beast as his agent, linking chapter 12 to chapter 13. The textual variant is minor for meaning but explains differing verse divisions in English Bibles.

The chapter is a theological history of the first-century conflict: faithful Israel gives birth to Messiah, whom Satan opposes through Herod and the cross; at the ascension Satan is cast down; the Jewish-Christian church is protected (the Pella flight) during the 3.5 years of the Jewish War, while Satan turns on the wider church through Nero. Gentry and Chilton stress that the time indicators of the book ('soon') point to these events.

Reads the chapter much like partial preterists, but treats the 'short time' and the woman's deliverance as culminating in AD 70, when the old-covenant age ended and the kingdom was fully established; critics note that this is tied to a broader denial of a future bodily return, which full preterists answer by arguing that the Parousia was spiritual and covenantal (Max King, Don Preston).

A panorama of church history: the dragon is pagan Rome; the casting down of the dragon is the overthrow of paganism under Constantine; the woman's flight is the faithful church's long obscurity during 1,260 years of papal supremacy; the flood represents barbarian invasions or persecutions (Elliott, Barnes).

The woman is Israel; the birth and ascension of Christ form a historical flashback, but the war in heaven, the woman's flight and the 1,260 days belong to the second half of the future seventieth week, when Satan, expelled from heaven, persecutes a Jewish remnant that God protects (Walvoord, Thomas). They note that the 1,260 days and 'time, times and half a time' are Daniel's half-week (Daniel 7:25; 12:7), which Jesus tied to the abomination of desolation and the flight to the mountains (Matthew 24:15-21), and that Michael's arising in Daniel 12:1 introduces an unparalleled time of distress for Daniel's people.

A timeless portrait of the church's whole existence between Christ's first and second comings: Satan, defeated at the cross, rages against God's people, who are spiritually protected and conquer by faith and witness even unto death (Hendriksen, Milligan). The compression of Christ's whole career into 12:5 shows that the decisive battle is already won; the wilderness, the eagle's wings and the nourishment for 1,260 days picture the whole church age as a new exodus in which God preserves his people.

Beale and others combine a redemptive-historical anchor (Christ's birth, cross and ascension as Satan's decisive defeat) with an idealist application across the church age and a final intensification before the end; Ladd likewise reads the inaugurated victory of the cross as leading to a future climax.
Why do you think John tells the story of Christ's birth and ascension in a single verse (12:5), and what does that omission of the life and cross of Jesus emphasise?
How does reading the woman as Israel, the church, or the whole people of God change how you understand her flight into the wilderness?
Revelation 12:11 says the saints conquer by the blood of the Lamb and their testimony. How does that redefine victory compared with Roman ideas of triumph?
Is the casting down of Satan in 12:9 the same event as the binding of Satan in 20:1-3? What is at stake for the millennial views?
What difference does it make whether the 1,260 days are read as literal days, years, or a symbol of the church age?
The Beast from the Sea and the Beast from the Land

Standing on the shore, the dragon calls up his agents. A seven-headed, ten-horned beast rises from the sea, combining the features of Daniel's four beasts; it receives the dragon's throne, survives a mortal wound, blasphemes God for 42 months and makes war on the saints, while all whose names are not in the Lamb's book of life worship it. A second beast rises from the earth, lamb-like but speaking like a dragon; it performs signs, sets up an image of the first beast that can speak and kill, and forces everyone to receive a mark on hand or forehead to buy or sell. John ends with a riddle: the number of the beast is the number of a man, 666.
The beast from the sea receives the dragon's authority
Blasphemy and war on the saints for 42 months; a call to endurance
The beast from the land and the speaking image
The mark of the beast and the number 666

Revelation 13 rewrites Daniel 7 for the church's situation. Daniel's four beasts from the sea (lion, bear, leopard and a ten-horned monster) become a single composite beast; the little horn's boastful mouth, its 3.5-year persecution and its war on the saints transfer directly (Daniel 7:8, 21, 25). The two beasts recall Leviathan and Behemoth, the sea and land monsters of Job 40-41 that Second Temple texts (1 Enoch 60, 4 Ezra 6, 2 Baruch 29) say God will defeat at the end. Daniel 3 (the golden image and the death penalty for refusing to worship it) and Deuteronomy 13 (false prophets with signs) shape the second half, while the mark on hand and forehead parodies the Shema's command to bind God's words there (Deuteronomy 6:8) and the seal of God in Revelation 7. The beast, false prophet and dragon form a counterfeit trinity, and the beast's 'slain yet living' head is a dark parody of the Lamb.

For first-century readers in Asia, the setting was the imperial cult. Temples to Roma and the emperors stood in Pergamum, Smyrna and Ephesus; local elites served as high priests and promoted emperor-worship in civic festivals, guild banquets and the marketplace; coins carried the emperor's image and divine titles. Nero was the first emperor to persecute Christians (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), died by the sword in 68, and was rumoured to be returning (the Nero redivivus legend and several false Neros). Pliny's letter to Trajan (c. 112) shows the test that later faced Christians in this province: offer incense before the emperor's image or die. How directly John alludes to Nero depends partly on the disputed date of Revelation (pre-70 or c. 95); even late-date scholars often see the Nero legend behind the healed wound and the number 666, while futurists see these as anticipations of a future Antichrist.
A beast rising out of the sea

Daniel 7:2-8 sees four beasts rising from the wind-churned great sea, representing successive empires, the fourth with ten horns and a boastful little horn. The sea monster Leviathan (Job 41; Isaiah 27:1) stands behind the image; 1 Enoch 60:7-9, 4 Ezra 6:49-52 and 2 Baruch 29:4 pair a female sea monster Leviathan with a male land monster Behemoth, a pairing John seems to adapt in the two beasts of chapter 13.

From the viewpoint of the seven churches, Roman power literally came from over the sea: the proconsul of Asia arrived by ship at Ephesus. The sea was also associated in Greek thought with chaos and the unruly masses (compare 17:15, 'waters' as peoples).

The beast is the dragon's agent on earth: a political power that demands worship and persecutes the saints. In the first readers' world it most naturally evoked imperial Rome. The interpretive dispute is whether it is limited to Rome, refers to a later institution, points to a future individual Antichrist, or is a symbol of idolatrous state power that recurs in every age (several of these can be combined).
Imperial Rome, which can be viewed corporately (the empire) or personified in its head Nero, the first emperor to persecute Christians (Gentry, Chilton).
As in partial preterism, Rome and Nero in the run-up to AD 70; all of the chapter is fulfilled in the first century.
The papacy as a politico-religious power that rose from the ruins of the western Roman empire and ruled for 1,260 years (Barnes, Elliott, and in Adventist form Uriah Smith).
The end-time Antichrist and his revived Roman or world empire, which will dominate during the final 3.5 years (Walvoord, Thomas).
The persecuting state that claims divine honours, manifest in Rome and in every later totalitarian power, culminating at the end (Hendriksen, Beale).
Ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads

Daniel's little horn speaks great things against the Most High (Daniel 7:8, 25), and Antiochus IV 'magnifies himself above every god' (Daniel 11:36), even calling himself Epiphanes ('God manifest') on coins.

Emperors bore titles that Jews and Christians regarded as blasphemous: divi filius ('son of the deified'), Augustus / Sebastos ('worthy of reverence'), soter (saviour), pontifex maximus, and, according to Suetonius (Domitian 13), Domitian liked to be called dominus et deus noster, 'our Lord and God'. Such titles were stamped on coins and inscribed on temples throughout Asia.

The beast's heads bear names that claim divine status for human rulers. Crowns on the horns (where the dragon had them on the heads) suggest that the beast's royal authority is exercised through many rulers.
Like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion

These are the first three beasts of Daniel 7:4-6 (lion, bear, leopard), listed here in reverse order. In Daniel they are usually understood as Babylon, Media-Persia and Greece (or Babylon, Media, Persia), followed by a fourth terrifying beast.

John's beast combines the features of all Daniel's empires, so it is the climax and summary of world-empire opposed to God. Listing them in reverse order suggests John looks back from his own time through history. Hosea 13:7-8 also uses lion, leopard and bear for God's judgment, a less-noticed echo.
The dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority

In Daniel 7 dominion is taken from the beasts and given to the son of man; here the dragon parodies God by delegating his throne to a rival 'son'. Satan offers Jesus the kingdoms of the world in Luke 4:5-7.

Pergamum, with its imperial temple to Roma and Augustus (29 BC), is called the place 'where Satan's throne is' (Revelation 2:13). Emperors claimed their authority from the gods; John says it comes from the dragon.

The beast's political power is real but derivative: Satan is the true power behind persecuting empire. This counterfeit trinity (dragon, beast, false prophet) parodies the Father, the Son and the Spirit.
One of its heads appeared to be mortally wounded, but the mortal wound was healed

The phrase 'as slain' (hos esphagmenen) deliberately mirrors the Lamb 'as slain' in Revelation 5:6: the beast imitates Christ's death and resurrection. Genesis 3:15 promised a crushing blow to the serpent's head, and some see the 'wound by the sword' (13:14) as God's judgment, which the beast survives for a time.

Nero killed himself with a sword (or had a freedman help him) in June 68 (Suetonius, Nero 49). Rumours soon spread that he was not dead or would return from the east with the Parthians; at least three impostors claimed to be Nero (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57), and the Sibylline Oracles (4.119-139; 5.137-154, 361-370) turned this into a Nero redivivus myth. The empire itself nearly collapsed in the civil wars of 68-69 (the Year of the Four Emperors) and then revived under Vespasian.

The beast suffers a fatal blow yet survives, provoking awe. Most scholars see some relation to the Nero legend; others see a parody of the resurrection with no single historical referent. Which head, which wound, and when it is healed are among the most debated details in the book.
The death of Nero (the head) brought Rome to the brink of collapse in 68-69; its recovery under Vespasian is the healing that made the world marvel (Gentry).

The fall of the pagan western empire in 476 (or of Roman imperial rule generally) healed when papal Rome revived its power; Adventist historicism adds the 1798 captivity of the pope and the later restoration of the Vatican's sovereignty in 1929 (Barnes, Smith).
Either an apparent death and recovery of the Antichrist himself, possibly a satanic counterfeit of resurrection, or the revival of the Roman empire in the end times (Walvoord, Thomas).
The beast was dealt a mortal blow by Christ's death and resurrection, yet state idolatry keeps reviving in new forms until the end (Beale, Hendriksen).
Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?

A parody of Israel's praise after the Red Sea, 'Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?' (Exodus 15:11; compare Psalm 35:10; 89:6-8; Micah 7:18), and of the name Michael ('Who is like God?'), whose victory was just narrated.

Imperial hymns and acclamations praised the emperor's invincibility; the Roman army seemed beyond resistance (compare Josephus's speech of Agrippa II urging Jews not to fight Rome, Jewish War 2.345-401).
The world's worship is driven by awe at military power. The irony is that Michael has already overcome the dragon whom the beast serves.
A mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, slandering God's name and His tabernacle

Daniel's little horn has 'a mouth speaking great things' (Daniel 7:8, 11, 20, 25) and the king of Daniel 11:36 speaks astonishing things against the God of gods. Antiochus profaned the temple; Caligula tried to set up his statue in Jerusalem's temple in 40 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.261-309; Philo, Embassy to Gaius).

Nero appeared on coins with the radiate crown of the sun god and was hailed as Apollo; temples to living or deified emperors filled Asia. Domitian's 'Lord and God' title (Suetonius, Domitian 13) is often cited.
Blasphemy is the beast's characteristic speech. Its slander of God's 'tabernacle, those who dwell in heaven' shows that God's dwelling is now his people (compare 21:3), whom the beast vilifies.
Authority to act for 42 months

The same 3.5-year period as Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 and Revelation 11:2 and 12:6, 14: the limited span of the persecutor's power. 'Was given' (edothe) appears repeatedly, stressing that God sets the limit.

Nero's persecution of Christians began after the great fire of Rome in July 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44) and ended with his death in June 68, roughly 42 months; partial preterists stress this match, while critics note the start date is approximate.
The beast's authority is real but limited and God-bounded.
The Neronic persecution from late 64 to June 68 (Gentry).
1,260 years of papal supremacy on the day-year principle (Barnes, Elliott, Smith).
The literal final 3.5 years of Daniel's seventieth week (Walvoord).
The church age as a limited time of trial (Hendriksen).
Permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them

A direct citation of Daniel 7:21, where the little horn makes war on the saints and prevails until the Ancient of Days comes. It also reverses Revelation 11:7 and anticipates the saints' true victory in 15:2.

Tacitus (Annals 15.44) records that under Nero 'a vast multitude' of Christians were arrested and executed, some burned as torches, some torn by dogs; later persecutions under Domitian are debated by historians, and Pliny (Letters 10.96) shows Christians executed in Asia by about 112.
The beast's victory is physical (martyrdom), but the saints' faithfulness is the real victory (12:11; 15:2). The verse warns that the church should expect suffering, not exemption.
Authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation
Nebuchadnezzar demanded that 'peoples, nations and languages' worship his golden image (Daniel 3:4, 7); John's fourfold formula also echoes the Lamb's redeemed from every tribe and tongue (5:9; 7:9).
Roman propaganda presented the empire as the oikoumene, the whole inhabited world; the Sebasteion at Aphrodisias displayed reliefs of the many conquered nations (ethne) under Rome.

The beast's claim to universal dominion counterfeits the Lamb's universal redemption. Whether 'every nation' is hyperbole for the Roman world or literally global is part of the wider interpretive dispute.
The Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain, from the foundation of the world

God's book of the living appears in Exodus 32:32-33, Psalm 69:28, Isaiah 4:3, Daniel 12:1 and Malachi 3:16; 1 Enoch 47:3 and 108:3 and Jubilees 30:22 speak of heavenly books of the righteous. Qumran texts likewise speak of those 'written' for life.
Greek cities kept citizen registers; a disgraced citizen's name could be erased (compare Revelation 3:5 to Sardis). Being inscribed meant belonging and rights.

Those secure in the Lamb's book do not worship the beast. The Greek word order allows 'from the foundation of the world' to modify 'written' (names written before creation, as in 17:8) or 'slain' (the Lamb slain in God's eternal purpose, compare 1 Peter 1:19-20). Translations and commentators divide; both readings affirm God's sovereign purpose of salvation.
If anyone is destined for captivity, into captivity he will go; if anyone is to die by the sword, by the sword he must be killed

Adapted from Jeremiah 15:2 and 43:11, where God's people are destined for death, sword, famine and captivity. Manuscripts differ in the second line: some read that whoever kills with the sword must be killed with the sword (compare Matthew 26:52), which makes it a warning against armed resistance or a promise of retribution.

The saying calls for patient endurance: believers should accept suffering as within God's sovereign plan and not take up the sword. The 'call for perseverance and faith' is the practical application of the whole chapter. The textual variant is genuinely uncertain and modern translations differ.
He who has an ear, let him hear
Echoes the hearing formula of Isaiah 6:9-10 and Ezekiel 3:27, used by Jesus with his parables (Matthew 13:9) and repeated in each of the seven letters (Revelation 2-3).

The formula links this vision to the letters to the churches: the beast's pressure is exactly the danger addressed there (Pergamum, Thyatira, Laodicea). Only those with spiritual insight will see through the beast's propaganda.
Another beast rising out of the earth

Behemoth, the land monster paired with Leviathan (Job 40:15-24; 1 Enoch 60:7-9; 4 Ezra 6:49-52). Later in the book this beast is called the 'false prophet' (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), recalling Deuteronomy 13:1-5, which warns against prophets who perform signs to lead Israel after other gods.

In Asia the imperial cult was promoted not from Rome but by local elites: the provincial council (koinon) of Asia, its high priests (archiereis), city magistrates and wealthy benefactors. Provincial temples to the emperors stood at Pergamum (to Roma and Augustus, 29 BC), Smyrna (to Tiberius, 26) and Ephesus (to the Sebastoi, c. 89/90, with a colossal statue of Titus or Domitian). 'Earth' could also mean 'the land', i.e. Judea, which some preterists stress.
A religious or ideological power that serves the political beast by promoting its worship through signs, propaganda and economic pressure. Identification depends on one's framework.

Either the provincial priesthood and elites of the imperial cult in Asia, or the Jewish high-priestly leadership in the land of Israel who aligned with Rome against Christ and his people (Gentry; Chilton reads it as the apostate Jewish leadership).

The papal clergy or spiritual power that promoted the authority of the papal beast (Barnes, Elliott); Seventh-day Adventist historicism identifies it with the United States, rising peacefully 'from the earth' (Smith).
A future individual, the false prophet, who will lead worldwide worship of the Antichrist (Walvoord, Thomas).
False religion, philosophy and propaganda in every age that persuade people to give ultimate loyalty to the state or culture (Hendriksen, Beale).
Two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon
Jesus warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15). Daniel's ram with two horns (Daniel 8:3, 20) may also lie in the background.
Imperial cult priests presented emperor worship as civic piety and benevolence, using the gentle language of peace (pax Romana) and benefaction.
The second beast looks harmless, even Christ-like, but its message is the dragon's. It is a counterfeit of the Lamb and a warning against deception within religious and cultural institutions.
Great signs, even fire from heaven to come down to earth

Elijah called down fire from heaven on Mount Carmel and on the king's soldiers (1 Kings 18:38; 2 Kings 1:10-12), and the two witnesses have fire from their mouths (Revelation 11:5). Pharaoh's magicians imitated Moses' signs (Exodus 7:11, 22). Deuteronomy 13 and Jesus (Mark 13:22) warn of deceptive signs.

Ancient temples staged marvels: hidden fires, automata (Hero of Alexandria described temple machines), and oracle tricks. Lucian's 'Alexander the False Prophet' satirises a 2nd-century Asia Minor prophet whose talking serpent-god Glycon drew crowds; Acts 8 and later legends depict Simon Magus as a wonder-worker.
The false prophet counterfeits prophetic power to authenticate the beast. Whether the signs are real demonic wonders or skilful trickery is debated; the text's point is that signs do not prove truth.
An image to the beast, given breath so that it could speak and cause those who refused to worship it to be killed

Nebuchadnezzar's golden image required worship on pain of death in the furnace (Daniel 3:1-15); Antiochus set up the 'abomination of desolation' (Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:54). The idols mocked in Psalm 115:5 and Habakkuk 2:18-19 have no breath; this one is given 'breath' (pneuma), a parody of God's life-giving Spirit (Genesis 2:7; Revelation 11:11).

Statues of emperors stood in temples, marketplaces and gymnasia across Asia. Around 112 Pliny tested accused Christians by requiring them to invoke the gods and offer incense and wine before the emperor's image and to curse Christ, executing those who persisted (Letters 10.96). Speaking statues produced by ventriloquism or hidden devices are reported in ancient sources.
The image represents enforced participation in idolatrous loyalty to the beast, with death for refusal. It is the crux of the chapter's call to faithful endurance.

The cult statues of the emperor in Asia and the demand to honour them, or (for those who see the land beast as Jewish leadership) the pressure on Christians to honour Caesar rather than Christ (Gentry).
The papal system's images and its enforced religious conformity, or an image of papal authority in a later political power (Barnes, Smith).
A literal image of the Antichrist, possibly technologically animated, set up in a rebuilt Jerusalem temple (Walvoord, Thomas).
Every idol of political or cultural power that society demands people honour (Hendriksen).
All people small and great, rich and poor, free and slave
Merisms like this express totality (compare Deuteronomy 1:17; Psalm 115:13; Revelation 11:18; 19:18; 20:12).
Roman society was tightly stratified by wealth and legal status; the beast's demand cuts through every class, and the list anticipates 6:15 and 19:18.
No one is exempt from the pressure to conform; the same categories appear at the final judgment, where every class stands before God (20:12).
A mark on their right hand or on their forehead

The beast's mark parodies God's seal on the foreheads of his servants (Revelation 7:3; 14:1) and the Lamb's and Father's name they bear. Ezekiel 9:4 marks the faithful with the letter tav on their foreheads. Deuteronomy 6:8 (the Shema) tells Israel to bind God's words on hand and forehead (the origin of tefillin), so the beast's mark claims the loyalty of thought and action that belongs to God. 3 Maccabees 2:29 reports that Ptolemy IV ordered Jews to be branded with the ivy-leaf of Dionysus, a striking precedent for a religious mark imposed by a king.

Charagma was the word for the imperial seal on contracts and for the stamped image on coins. Slaves, soldiers and temple devotees could be branded or tattooed (stigmata) as property of a master or god. Later (250) Decius required certificates of sacrifice (libelli) to prove loyalty, a later but illuminating parallel.

The mark signifies ownership and allegiance to the beast, in contrast to God's seal. Most scholars read it symbolically (just as God's seal is not a visible tattoo), while some insist on a literal, visible mark. Either way it is a matter of worship, not an accidental technology.

Visible allegiance to Caesar or the imperial system, shown in conduct and in participation in civic cult and trade (Gentry); some preterists link it to the Roman coinage bearing the emperor's image and name.

Profession of allegiance to the papal system; Seventh-day Adventist historicism adds the enforcement of Sunday observance in place of the seventh-day Sabbath (Smith); most Protestant historicists read it as conformity to Rome's doctrine and worship (Barnes).

A literal identifying mark that will be required for commerce under the Antichrist; many futurists note modern technologies could make this feasible, while warning against date-setting (Walvoord, Thomas).
A symbol of the mindset (forehead) and actions (hand) of those who give ultimate loyalty to the world-system, the counterpart of God's seal on believers (Hendriksen, Beale).
No one could buy or sell unless he had the mark

Economic exclusion of the faithful appears in Jewish tradition (e.g. pressures under Antiochus in 1 Maccabees); Israel's prophets condemned commerce built on idolatry and injustice (Ezekiel 27-28; Amos 8:4-6).

In the cities of Asia, trade guilds (collegia) held meals in honour of patron gods and the emperor; refusing participation could mean economic isolation, which is probably the issue behind the 'Jezebel' controversy at Thyatira (2:20). Roman coins carried the emperor's image and divine titles (compare Mark 12:16).

Loyalty to the beast is enforced economically as well as politically. For the first readers this was a lived reality; John's call is to accept economic loss rather than compromise. Revelation 18 later shows the merchants who profited from Babylon lamenting her fall.
The number of the beast: the number of a man, and that number is 666

Hebrew and Greek letters doubled as numerals, so every name had a numerical value (gematria in Hebrew, isopsephy in Greek). Jewish and Christian writers used it: the Sibylline Oracles (1.324-330) give the value of Jesus' name (Iesous) as 888, and later rabbis used gematria in interpretation. Solomon received 666 talents of gold a year (1 Kings 10:14; 2 Chronicles 9:13) just before his turn to idolatry, which some see as a background. 'Here is wisdom' echoes Daniel's wise who understand (Daniel 12:10).
